title: What is the difference between caching/persistence and checkpointing (cache = reuse optimization, lineage preserved; checkpoint = materialize to reliable storage and truncate lineage for fault recovery)?

s1_definition.profdef: Caching or persistence and checkpointing both materialize a dataset to avoid recomputation, but they differ in purpose, storage, and effect on lineage. Caching is a reuse optimization: it stores computed partitions on executors, in memory or on local disk, and preserves the lineage so that if a cached partition is lost it is recomputed from its parents. Checkpointing is a fault-recovery mechanism: it writes the dataset to reliable, replicated storage such as HDFS and truncates the lineage, so recovery and future computation start from the checkpoint rather than replaying the entire chain.
s1_definition.analogy: Both are ways the clerk at the National Bank of India keeps a finished summary instead of rebuilding it. Caching is keeping it on his own desk or in his local drawer — fast to reuse, but it is not truly safe, and he still keeps the recipe so he can rebuild it if his desk is cleared. Checkpointing is taking the finished summary down to the bank's central vault, which is fireproof and backed up, and then tearing up the long recipe because he will never need to rebuild from scratch again — the vault copy is the new starting point. Caching optimizes speed and keeps the recipe; checkpointing guarantees durability and throws the long recipe away.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cache keeps data on executors for fast reuse and preserves lineage, while checkpoint writes data to reliable storage and truncates lineage for durable fault recovery.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Caching or persistence and checkpointing both materialize a dataset to avoid recomputation, but they differ in purpose, storage, and effect on lineage. Caching is a reuse optimization: it stores computed partitions on executors, in memory or on local disk, and preserves the lineage so that if a cached partition is lost it is recomputed from its parents. Checkpointing is a fault-recovery mechanism: it writes the dataset to reliable, replicated storage such as HDFS and truncates the lineage, so recovery and future computation start from the checkpoint rather than replaying the entire chain.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Both are ways the clerk at the National Bank of India keeps a finished summary instead of rebuilding it. Caching is keeping it on his own desk or in his local drawer — fast to reuse, but it is not truly safe, and he still keeps the recipe so he can rebuild it if his desk is cleared. Checkpointing is taking the finished summary down to the bank's central vault, which is fireproof and backed up, and then tearing up the long recipe because he will never need to rebuild from scratch again — the vault copy is the new starting point. Caching optimizes speed and keeps the recipe; checkpointing guarantees durability and throws the long recipe away.

**One line to remember:** Cache keeps data on executors for fast reuse and preserves lineage, while checkpoint writes data to reliable storage and truncates lineage for durable fault recovery.

sections.s2_technical:
Caching and persistence are performance optimizations. They store a dataset's computed partitions on the executors — in memory by default, optionally spilling to local disk — so that repeated actions reuse them instead of recomputing. Crucially, caching preserves the lineage: Spark still remembers the full chain of transformations that produced the dataset, because a cached partition is not guaranteed to survive. If an executor dies or memory pressure evicts a partition, Spark transparently recomputes it from that preserved lineage. So caching speeds up reuse but does nothing to shorten the lineage and offers no durability guarantee on its own — it is fast but fragile.

Checkpointing is a durability and lineage-management mechanism. It writes the dataset's partitions to reliable, replicated storage, typically a distributed file system like HDFS or cloud storage, which survives executor and node failures. Having done that, Spark truncates the lineage of the checkpointed dataset: it discards the record of how the dataset was derived and treats the checkpoint files as the new source. This is the key difference — checkpointing deliberately cuts the lineage, whereas caching deliberately keeps it. The cost is that checkpointing is expensive: it writes all the data out to reliable storage, and it triggers a computation to do so.

The reason lineage truncation matters is iterative and long-lineage workloads. In iterative algorithms, each iteration adds to the lineage, so after many iterations the chain becomes enormous, and any recomputation or even just planning over that giant lineage becomes slow and memory-heavy, sometimes causing stack overflows in the scheduler. Checkpointing periodically cuts this chain so it cannot grow without bound, which keeps the application stable. Caching cannot do this because it keeps the lineage intact.

A senior nuance is that the two are complementary and often used together. Because checkpointing triggers a computation to write the data, a common pattern is to cache a dataset and then checkpoint it, so the checkpoint write reads from the cache rather than recomputing the whole lineage, and the cached copy still serves fast reuse afterward. Reliable checkpointing is what you want for fault recovery and lineage truncation; there is also a lighter local checkpoint that truncates lineage using local disk without the reliability guarantee, which is faster but not fault tolerant. The decision rule I use is: cache for speed when a dataset is reused, and checkpoint when the lineage is dangerously long or when I need the dataset to survive failures durably. In the bank, we cached shared reporting datasets for reuse, but for long iterative risk-model computations we checkpointed periodically to HDFS so a failure did not replay hundreds of iterations and the scheduler did not choke on an ever-growing lineage.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A reused dataset should be fast to read but can be rebuilt if lost. This is exactly caching with preserved lineage.

Problem 2 — An iterative computation's lineage grows unboundedly and recovery gets slow. This is exactly what checkpointing's lineage truncation fixes.

Problem 3 — Checkpointing recomputes unless the data is already cached. This is exactly why cache-then-checkpoint is the common pattern.

The mini-project models both in Java. A `Dataset` tracks its lineage depth, supports `cache()` which stores on executors and keeps lineage, and `checkpoint()` which writes to a reliable store and resets lineage depth to zero. The demo runs an iterative aggregation over Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, showing the lineage growing, caching for reuse, and checkpointing to truncate it, with a simulated failure recovered from the checkpoint.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a risk-model aggregate seeded at one million rupees, iterated fifty times in a loop, which grows the lineage to depth fifty.

Step 1: After fifty iterations the dataset's value has grown through the iterative update, and its lineage depth is fifty, meaning any recomputation or planning must replay fifty steps. This long lineage is the danger in iterative workloads.

Step 2: The dataset is cached. This stores the current partitions on the executors for fast reuse, but it preserves the lineage at depth fifty, because caching is a performance optimization and a cached partition could still be lost and recomputed.

Step 3: The dataset is then checkpointed. Because it was cached first, the checkpoint write reads from the cache rather than recomputing the whole fifty-step lineage, which is the cache-then-checkpoint pattern that avoids a double computation.

Step 4: Checkpointing writes the value to the reliable store, which survives node failures, and then truncates the lineage to depth zero, treating the checkpoint as the new source. The dangerous fifty-step chain is gone.

Step 5: The loop continues for ten more iterations, and the lineage grows from zero to ten rather than from fifty to sixty, so the checkpoint has bounded the lineage growth, keeping the scheduler and any recovery fast.

Step 6: A failure is simulated and recovery runs. Because a checkpoint exists in reliable storage, recovery reads the durable value directly with lineage depth zero, rather than replaying iterations. The journey shows caching giving fast reuse while keeping lineage, and checkpointing giving durability while truncating lineage.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] after 50 iterations: lineage depth=50, value=117390852
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] cache(): stored on executors, lineage PRESERVED (depth=50), not durable
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] checkpoint reads from CACHE (no full recompute) — cache-then-checkpoint
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] CHECKPOINT written to reliable store: risk_model_iter50=117390852
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] checkpoint(): lineage TRUNCATED to depth=0 (reliable copy is new source)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] after 10 more: lineage depth=10 (bounded thanks to checkpoint)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] recover from CHECKPOINT (reliable store), depth=0, value=117390852
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  iterate x50 → lineage depth = 50 (DANGEROUS long chain)
    │
    ▼  cache()   → store on executors, lineage KEPT (fast reuse, fragile)
    │
    ▼  checkpoint("risk_model_iter50")
    ├─ reads from CACHE (no full recompute)  ← cache-then-checkpoint
    ├─ writes value to RELIABLE store (HDFS, survives node loss)
    └─ TRUNCATE lineage → depth = 0 (checkpoint is new source)
    │
    ▼  iterate x10 → lineage depth = 10 (bounded, not 60)
    │
    ▼  FAILURE → recover()
  checkpoint exists → read reliable store, depth=0  (no replay of 50 iterations)

  cache = speed + lineage kept ; checkpoint = durability + lineage cut
```

```text
  ┌──────────┐ cache  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Driver   │───────→│ Executors: cached partitions   │ ← fast reuse, lineage kept
  │          │        │ (memory/local disk, fragile)   │
  │          │        └────────────────────────────────┘
  │          │ checkpoint
  │          │        ┌────────────────────────────────┐

  recover: cached lost → recompute from lineage ;

  Observability: Storage tab (cache) ; checkpoint dir size (checkpoint)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Caching and checkpointing both materialize a dataset to avoid recomputation, but they serve different purposes and differ fundamentally in how they treat lineage. Caching, or persistence, is a performance optimization: it stores a dataset's computed partitions on the executors, in memory by default and optionally on local disk, so repeated actions reuse them. Critically, caching preserves the lineage, because a cached partition is not guaranteed to survive — if an executor dies or memory pressure evicts it, Spark transparently recomputes it from the lineage. So caching is fast but fragile, and it offers no durability on its own and does nothing to shorten the lineage.

Checkpointing is a durability and lineage-management mechanism. It writes the dataset to reliable, replicated storage like HDFS or cloud storage that survives node failures, and then it truncates the lineage, discarding the record of how the dataset was derived and treating the checkpoint files as the new source. That lineage truncation is the key difference — caching deliberately keeps the lineage, checkpointing deliberately cuts it. This matters most in iterative and long-lineage workloads, where each iteration extends the chain until recomputation or even scheduler planning over that giant lineage becomes slow and memory-heavy, sometimes causing stack overflows; checkpointing periodically cuts the chain so it cannot grow without bound. The cost is that checkpointing is expensive, because it writes all the data to reliable storage and triggers a computation to do so.

In my project at the National Bank of India I used them together following the common cache-then-checkpoint pattern. We cached shared reporting datasets purely for fast reuse, but for long iterative risk-model computations we checkpointed periodically to HDFS, and we always cached before checkpointing so that the checkpoint write read from the cache instead of recomputing the whole lineage, and the cached copy still served fast reuse afterward. The decision rule I state is simple: cache for speed when a dataset is reused, and checkpoint when the lineage is dangerously long or when the dataset must survive failures durably. Checkpointing meant a failure in a hundred-iteration risk job did not replay all those iterations, and the scheduler never choked on an ever-growing lineage.
